finding.claim: Expired-token acceptance from the verification cache. When a token has `exp` but no numeric `iat` (for example one signed with `noTimestamp`), `cacheSet` skips the whole exp/nbf block because it is nested under `if (hasIat)`. The cached entry's expiry is then `clockTimestamp + clockTolerance + cacheTTL`, which is 10 minutes by default. A token whose `exp` is only seconds away keeps being returned as valid from the cache after it has expired. An attacker holding a captured or leaked short-lived token can replay it for up to `cacheTTL` after `exp`. This only applies when caching is enabled and the issuer omits `iat`.
finding.source: A signed token with `exp` and no `iat`, sent to a verifier created with the `cache` option. The cache is on by default only when `cache` is set, so this is a precondition on the deployment.
finding.sink: The cache hit path at src/verifier.js:363-378 returns the cached payload as success without re-checking `exp`.

trace.note: A cache lookup keyed by the hash of the token runs before any decode or validation.
After the first successful verification, cacheSet is called with the payload.
`hasIat` is false when `payload.iat` is not a number.
The nbf and exp handling is only inside `if (hasIat)`, so `cacheValue[2]` stays 0.
Because `cacheValue[2]` is 0, it becomes `maxTTL` rather than being capped by `exp`.
A later request passes the check at this line because `min === 0` and `now <= max`, even though `payload.exp` has passed.
The cached payload is returned as valid.

finding.guards_checked: I checked the `exp` validator in verifyToken (src/verifier.js:304-323). It runs only on a cache miss, so it does not protect the cache-hit path. I found no `exp` check after the cache hit, and the cap against `exp` in cacheSet is applied only when `iat` is a number. Because `iat` is absent, `cacheValue[2]` remains 0 and is replaced by `maxTTL` at line 134. I did not run this; the finding comes from reading the code.
